question_text: Evaluate the nature of the Bhakti literature and its contribution to Indian culture. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Devotion in the people's language
It challenged ritual monopoly
It fed later language and a shared culture
Contribution is social as well as religious

points.text: Bhakti literature is devotion written in regional languages, not only a Sanskrit ritual text.
Its nature is personal, emotional and often critical of caste barriers and empty ritual.
It created and enriched modern Indian languages and a shared stock of song and story.
It widened who could take part in religious life, including women and lower castes.
Its contribution is a more accessible religious culture and a literary base that later public life used.

question_text: Trace the rise and growth of socio-religious reform movements with special reference to Young Bengal and Brahmo Samaj. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Reform began as a reply to colonial critique and internal decay
Brahmo Samaj rationalised worship and opposed sati-type custom
Young Bengal was more radical and less rooted
Growth was urban, elite and uneven

points.text: Nineteenth-century reform grew from contact with Western education and a felt decay in social practice.
Brahmo Samaj, from Rammohan Roy, stood for a rational theism, an end to sati and a wider education.
Young Bengal, around Derozio, pushed free thought harder and shocked custom, but stayed a small Calcutta circle.
Both prepared a public that could argue religion and social reform in print.
The movements rose in the colonial city and grew as idea more than as a mass organisation.

question_text: Assess the main administrative issues and socio-cultural problems in the integration process of Indian Princely States. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Hundreds of states had to accede
Administration, army and finance had to be merged
People, language and a ruler's pride were the social problems
The process was political, not only a form

points.text: About 565 princely states had to be brought into the Union after 1947.
Administrative issues were accession, merger of services, privy purses and demobilising private armies.
Socio-cultural problems were a ruler's prestige, a people's identity and the joining of very unequal units.
Hyderabad, Junagadh and Jammu and Kashmir showed that consent was not always smooth.
Integration succeeded, but it left administrative hangovers and some unsettled identities.

question_text: Differentiate the causes of landslides in the Himalayan region and Western Ghats. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Landslides in the Himalaya and Western Ghats
topics: Landslides in the Himalaya and Western Ghats
keyPointers: Himalaya: young rock, quake and a steep slope
Western Ghats: laterite, heavy rain and a cut slope
Both are worsened by road and building
The trigger differs by geology

points.text: Both belts slide, but the cause is not the same.
The Himalaya is young, fractured and seismic; a quake and a cloudburst start large slides.
The Western Ghats fail more from intense rain on laterite and on slopes cut for road, quarry and plantation.
Human load matters in both, but tectonic energy is the Himalayan extra.
Mitigation has to follow the local cause, not one national recipe.

question_text: Despite India being one of the countries of the Gondwanaland, its mining industry contributes much less to its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in percentage. Discuss. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: The rock heritage is not the same as an industry
Most value is raw export or unused reserve
Regulation, a forest and a low technology keep the share small
GDP percentage is not the same as importance

points.text: A Gondwana geology gave India coal and minerals; it did not automatically give a large mining GDP.
Much of the output is low-value raw material, and services now dominate the measured economy.
A slow lease, a forest clearance and illegal mining keep formal output and value addition low.
The sector's jobs and energy role are larger than its percentage of GDP.
The small share is a failure of value addition and governance, not a lack of rock.

question_text: What are the environmental implications of the reclamation of water bodies into urban land use? Explain with examples. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: A lake becomes a building and a flood
Groundwater and a wetland species go with it
Examples are Indian cities, not a theory
The implication is the next heavy rain

points.text: Filling a lake or a drain for housing removes the city's natural sponge.
The implication is flood, a falling water table and loss of a wetland bird and a fishery.
Chennai's tanks, Bengaluru's lakes and the floodplain of Delhi show the pattern.
Pollution is pushed downstream because the water body no longer holds and cleans a flow.
Urban land gained this way is paid for in the next flood.

question_text: Mention the global occurrence of volcanic eruptions in 2021 and their impact on regional environment. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: La Soufrière, Nyiragongo, La Palma and an Icelandic fissure
Ash, gas and lava are the local impact
Aviation and a settlement feel it first
2021 was a cluster, not one famous blast

points.text: 2021 had several notable eruptions, not one global event.
La Soufrière in St Vincent, Nyiragongo in the D.R. Congo, Cumbre Vieja on La Palma and Fagradalsfjall in Iceland were the main ones.
Ash disrupted air and crops; lava buried houses on La Palma; gas and a fast lava threatened Goma.
A regional climate effect was small; the local environment and the displaced people were the impact.
The year shows volcano risk is local and uneven, and warning saved some lives.

question_text: Why is India considered as a subcontinent? Elaborate your answer. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Size, a plate and a mountain wall
A climate of its own
Cultural variety follows the physical unit
Subcontinent is geography, not a political claim

points.text: India is called a subcontinent because it is a large, distinct physical unit inside Asia.
The Himalaya, the ocean on three sides and its own plate mark it off.
It has its own monsoon and a range of climates a single country rarely holds.
The physical separation also shaped a long, varied civilisation.
The term is geographical: size plus a clear natural boundary.

question_text: Examine the uniqueness of tribal knowledge system when compared with mainstream knowledge and cultural systems. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: It is oral, local and tied to a forest
Mainstream knowledge is written, general and institutional
Uniqueness is the relation to land, not a lack of science
It is vulnerable when the forest goes

points.text: Tribal knowledge is a tested practice held in a community, not a textbook system.
It is oral, place-bound and organised around a forest, a seed and a season.
Mainstream systems are written, specialised and backed by a state and a university.
The uniqueness is ecological fit and a shared ownership, which a patent culture often misses.
It should be recognised as knowledge, and it dies if the habitat and the language die.

question_text: Examine the role of 'Gig Economy' in the process of empowerment of women in India. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: A flexible entry to paid work
No security, no care support
Empowerment only if the earning is hers
The role is partial

points.text: Gig work lets some women earn without a full-time office.
Flexibility helps where a care duty or a family bar blocks a regular job.
Pay is unstable, social security is thin and the platform can control the worker.
Empowerment is real only when the income and the decision stay with the woman.
The gig economy opens a door; it does not by itself empower.

question_text: To what extent did the role of the Moderates prepare a base for the wider freedom movement? Comment. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: The Moderates and the freedom movement
topics: The Moderates and the freedom movement
keyPointers: They built a national platform and a critique
Their method was petition and an elite public
The base was ideas and organisation, not a mass
Extent: necessary, and not sufficient

points.text: The Moderates did not win freedom, but they made a national politics possible.
Congress, a press and a documented critique of drain and an unrepresentative rule were their base.
They trained a generation in constitutional method and linked provinces.
The limit was a narrow social base and a faith in British justice that later failed.
Extremists and Gandhi used that platform and went beyond it.
To a large extent they prepared the base; the wider movement needed a method they would not use.

question_text: Bring out the constructive programmes of Mahatma Gandhi during Non-Cooperation Movement and Civil Disobedience Movement. (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: Khadi, a village industry and Hindu-Muslim unity
Removal of untouchability and a basic education
The programme ran beside the protest
It was meant to build the society the movement wanted

points.text: Gandhi paired withdrawal of cooperation with a constructive build-up of Indian life.
During Non-Cooperation: khadi, national schools, a boycott that was also a village industry, and Hindu-Muslim unity.
During Civil Disobedience: salt as a people's act, plus continued khadi, anti-untouchability and prohibition.
The programme trained cadres when a movement was paused and gave the poor a role.
Constructive work was not a side activity; it was the society the struggle was practising.

question_text: "There arose a serious challenge to the Democratic State System between the two World Wars." Evaluate the statement. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Crisis of democracy between the wars
topics: Crisis of democracy between the wars
keyPointers: Fascism, Nazism and a depression
New democracies were fragile
The challenge was real and not universal
Evaluate: serious, and not the end of every democracy

points.text: Between 1919 and 1939 many new democracies failed and authoritarian regimes rose.
Italy, Germany, Japan and parts of eastern Europe replaced a parliament with a leader and a party.
War trauma, a depression and a fear of revolution were the conditions.
Britain, France and the United States kept elected government, so the challenge was serious but not total.
The statement holds: the democratic state was under a real, and in many places successful, attack.

question_text: Briefly mention the alignment of major mountain ranges of the world and explain their impact on local weather conditions, with examples. (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: Ranges run as belts: Andes, Rockies, Himalaya, Alps
A windward rain and a rain shadow
Alignment decides which slope is wet
Local weather is the barrier, not only the height

points.text: Major ranges are long barriers aligned with a plate boundary.
The Andes and the Rockies run north-south; the Himalaya and the Alps run broadly east-west.
A range across the wind forces a rise, a rain on the windward side and a dry lee, as in the Western Ghats and the Deccan.
The Himalaya blocks a cold northern wind and helps hold the monsoon.
Alignment, more than height alone, decides the local wet and dry.

question_text: How do the melting of the Arctic ice and glaciers of the Antarctic differently affect the weather patterns and human activities on the Earth? Explain. (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: Arctic loss is sea ice; Antarctic loss is land ice
Sea ice changes weather; land ice changes sea level
Human effects differ: shipping and a coast
They are not the same melt

points.text: Arctic melting is mostly sea ice; Antarctic melting that matters for the sea is land ice.
Less Arctic ice warms the north faster, shifts a jet stream and opens a shipping season.
Antarctic glacier loss adds water to the ocean and raises a sea level that threatens a coast far away.
Weather patterns feel the Arctic more directly; human settlement feels the Antarctic through the sea.
The difference is sea ice versus land ice, and therefore weather versus sea level.

question_text: Discuss the multi-dimensional implications of uneven distribution of mineral oil in the world. (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: A few regions hold the reserve
Trade, a price and a war follow
Importers and exporters live different risks
The dimension is political and economic, not only a map

points.text: Oil is concentrated in a few basins, so most countries must buy it.
Economic implication: a price shock hits an importer's inflation and an exporter's budget.
Political implication: alliances, a sanction and a conflict cluster around the fields and the routes.
Environmental implication: the producer bears the local damage; the consumer bears the carbon.
Uneven oil is a map that organises trade, power and vulnerability.

question_text: What are the main socio-economic implications arising out of the development of IT industries in major cities of India? (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: A new middle class and a migrant professional
Rent, a gated life and a strained city service
The gain is uneven inside the city
Implication is social as well as a salary

points.text: IT clusters in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and the NCR created a new urban class.
Incomes, a service job for women and a private school demand rose around the parks.
Rent, traffic and a water stress rose for everyone, including those outside the salary.
A dual city appeared: a campus economy beside an informal settlement that serves it.
The implication is growth with a sharper urban inequality.

question_text: Discuss the main objectives of Population Education and point out the measures to achieve them in India in detail. (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: Understand population, not only 'control'
Health, a small family and a responsible parenthood
Measures: school, a health worker and a later marriage
Achievement is a decision, not a slogan

points.text: Population education aims at an informed decision about family, health and resources.
Objectives: understand why numbers grow, the link to health and a job, and reject a coercive myth.
Measures: it in the school curriculum, a health worker, and a focus on the adolescent and the woman.
Delaying marriage, spacing and a reliable contraceptive service are the practical side.
In India the aim is reached when the choice is informed, especially for girls, not when a target is announced.

question_text: What is Cryptocurrency? How does it affect global society? Has it been affecting Indian society also? (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: A digital token on a shared ledger
Global effects: a payment outside a bank, a speculation and a crime
India feels it as investment, a scam and a policy fight
Society is affected before the law settles

points.text: A cryptocurrency is a digital token recorded on a shared ledger, not a note of a central bank.
Globally it offers a payment that crosses a border and a speculation that can wipe a saving.
It also eases a ransom, a laundering and a heavy energy use.
In India it has drawn young investors, a fraud and a debate on tax and a possible official digital currency.
Yes, Indian society is already affected, mainly as a risky asset and a regulatory gap.

question_text: How does Indian society maintain continuity in traditional social values? Enumerate the changes taking place in it. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Continuity and change in social values
topics: Continuity and change in social values
keyPointers: Family, a rite and a language carry the old value
Education, the city and the market change it
Continuity is selective
Enumerate both, do not choose one

points.text: Indian society keeps older values by repeating them in family, rite and language, while daily life changes them.
Continuity: respect for elders, a caste memory, a festival and a duty to the family.
Change: a nuclear household, women's education and work, a love marriage at the margin, and a consumer individual.
The city and the phone speed the change; the village and the rite slow it.
Continuity is real and selective; the change is in who decides inside the family.
